headline: Monhegan Ledges: Pollock Up Top, Cod Down Deep, Bass Tucked in the Rivers
subhead: Forty feet of clean water off Monhegan and a mackerel run that won't quit — but the stripers want the rivers this week, not the open bay.
body_markdown:
Had a fella at the co-op Tuesday morning, hauling gear off a skiff he'd borrowed from his brother-in-law, tell me he'd fished the outer ledges at Monhegan for three hours and never touched bottom once because the pollock wouldn't let his jig get there. That's the kind of problem I like hearing about. Told him that's about right for early August — the bait balls up top, the pollock follow, and you can forget the cod jig till you've had your fun on the surface first.

That's been the story most of this week out around Monhegan. Anchor or drift the ledges on the south and east side — 40 to 60 feet of water, tide running — and you'll find pollock schooled up chasing mackerel and herring right in the top 15 feet. A white or chartreuse diamond jig, or even a bare Sabiki string if you want to load the cooler fast, will get bit as soon as it hits water. Once that surface bite settles, which it usually does an hour either side of the tide change, drop down to 70-90 feet on the deeper humps off the island's north end and you'll pick up cod, mostly school-size, some pushing 10-15 pounds, on a jig tipped with a strip of mackerel belly. Haddock have been scarce inshore — that's a deeper-water fish this time of year, and the ones I've heard of came from the basin between Matinicus and the Rockland dumping grounds, 150 feet or better, on the bottom.

Mackerel themselves have been thick right along the whole run from Boothbay out to Eastern Egg Rock. If you want bait or just want to bend a rod with a kid aboard, three or four gold hooks and a bit of chum off the Cuckolds or around The Hypocrites will keep you busy till your arm's tired. The birds tell the story out there too — terns and puffins working the surface off Egg Rock most mornings, which means the sand eels and mackerel are stacked shallow, and that's drawing bass in tight to feed as well.

Speaking of bass — that's been the tricky part of the week. Penobscot Bay proper has been quieter than I'd like for August. The stripers are around, but they're not holding on the open ledges and rockpiles the way they will later this month. Right now the better fish are tucked into the river mouths — the Sheepscot, the Damariscotta, up around Wiscasset and the mouth of the Kennebec corridor — working the last two hours of the ebb when bait gets flushed out of the marsh creeks into cooler, cleaner water. A 4-inch olive or white soft-plastic swimbait on a 3/8-ounce jighead, worked slow along the current seams where the river water meets the salt, has been the most consistent producer. A few schoolies mixed with some solid 28-30 inch fish, nothing huge, but honest fish and steady enough to make an evening trip worthwhile.

We flagged this pattern last week — said to expect a stable, seasonal read across the zone — and that's exactly what's held. Nothing dramatic, no big temperature swing, no wind event to stir things up. Just Maine doing its steady August thing while the rest of the coast deals with warmer water pushing fish deeper or forcing a night bite. Up here we're still getting daylight action on bass because the Gulf of Maine keeps the whole system a few degrees cooler than folks are dealing with south of the Cape. That's worth remembering if you're used to fishing further down the coast — don't wait for dark up here, fish the tide instead.

Down around Deer Isle and Stonington, the groundfish pattern's holding too. The channel between Deer Isle and Isle au Haut, 80 to 120 feet depending where you drop, has been giving up pollock and the occasional keeper cod on jigs worked just off bottom during the last of the incoming tide. Bluefish have shown in small pods around the outer islands off Stonington, chopping bait on the surface in the afternoons — nothing like the blitzes you hear about further south, but enough 2-3 pound choppers to keep a spinning rod busy if you find the right slick of bait.

Vinalhaven and the deeper basin north of it toward North Haven remain a decent bet for anyone wanting a mixed bag — cod, pollock, and the odd haddock showing on the sounder in that 140-180 foot range. Slow-pitch jigging with a 6-8 ounce metal has been outproducing bait rigs down there this week, mostly because the current's been running harder than usual on the bigger tides, and the jig gets down and stays down better than bait on a hi-lo.

Looking ahead, I don't see much reason for this pattern to break. Winds have stayed manageable, no big blow forecast, and the bait's holding thick enough that both the bass and the groundfish have plenty to eat without having to move far. If you're planning a trip this week, I'd fish the rivers on the ebb for bass in the morning, then run out to Monhegan or the outer ledges midday when the tide's slack enough to fish comfortably, and clean up on pollock and mackerel while you're out there. By late August, once the bay starts cooling down at night, I expect the bass to spread back out onto the open structure — but for now, the rivers are where the smart money's fishing.
